title: Lesson 1: Loving Your Neighbors
description: Jesus said the second great commandment is like the first: love your neighbor as yourself. Through the Good Samaritan, you will see how Jesus turned the question around, from who counts as my neighbor to whom I will move toward, and how He crossed the road to you first.

blocks.text: Growing Deep gave you the foundations of life with God: the Father who runs toward you, the Son who covers you, and the Spirit who guides you. Now in Growing Up, that love starts to reach the people around you, beginning with the person God has placed right next to you.

blocks.alt: Growing Together Discipleship Series: Growing Up in Discipleship highlighted.
A Samaritan kneeling in the dirt beside a wounded stranger on a desolate road

blocks.title: The Good Samaritan
blocks.text:
A religious law teacher once stood up to test Jesus. "What shall I do to inherit eternal life?" Jesus asked him what the Law said, and the man answered with the two great commandments: love God with everything you are, and love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus told him he had answered correctly. But the man wanted to justify himself, so he asked, "And who is my neighbor?" Jesus answered with a story.

A traveler on the lonely road from Jerusalem to Jericho was attacked, stripped, beaten, and left half dead.

A priest came by, saw him, and passed by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, did the same. These were not evil men. They had important religious work waiting for them, and they kept walking.

Then a Samaritan came. Jews and Samaritans had despised each other for centuries, so a Jewish audience would have expected the Samaritan to be the villain, not the hero. Instead, he saw the man, had compassion, and went to him. He knelt in the dirt beside someone who, by every cultural standard, was his enemy. He poured oil and wine on the wounds, lifted the man onto his own animal, carried him to an inn, and paid for his care out of his own pocket.

Then Jesus asked, "Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?" The law teacher said, "The one who showed him mercy." And Jesus said, "You go, and do likewise." (Luke 10:25-37)
Hold onto that picture: the wounded man, the two who stepped to the far side, and the enemy kneeling in the dust. It ends in a place you may not expect.
1.1 - Which of the three travelers do you most resemble in your daily life right now: the priest with too much to do, the Levite who looks and keeps walking, or the one who stops?
The Second Is Like the First
When a religious leader asked Jesus which command mattered most, Jesus did not give a list. He gave two.

And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

Jesus called the second commandment like the first. Not lesser. Not optional. Loving God and loving the person next to you are one love pointed in two directions. And the order matters. You do not love your neighbor out of an empty tank. You give away what the Father has already poured into you.
Love Your Neighbor as Yourself

Notice the phrase Jesus tucked into the command: as yourself. Jesus is not shaming you for caring about your own life. He is using something you already do well. You think about your meals, your safety, your comfort, and your good name. Jesus knew exactly how much you love yourself, and He made that the measuring stick. He pointed at the love you already aim at yourself every day and said, aim some of that at your neighbor.
He said the same thing another way in the Sermon on the Mount, in what has come to be called the Golden Rule.
So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

Picture the treatment you long to receive: patience when you are tired, grace when you mess up, a real hello from someone who sees you. Then give that to others before they earn it or ask. Paul takes it one step further.
Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.

Humility here does not mean hating yourself. It means letting someone else's good matter to you as much as your own. Paul's very next words point to Jesus, who did not cling to His own rights but humbled Himself all the way to the cross (Philippians 2:5-8). The love He asks you to give is the love He has already shown you.
1.2 - Think about how much attention you naturally give to your own well-being in a normal day. What would change in your week if you gave the person next to you that same kind of attention?
Who Is My Neighbor?

The law teacher already knew the right answer. His problem was the question that came next. He wanted Jesus to draw a small circle so he could safely ignore everyone outside of it. Most of us have asked some version of his question. Who actually counts? Who can I leave off?

Jesus answered with the story, then flipped the question. The law teacher asked, "Who is my neighbor?" meaning, "Which people qualify for my love?" Jesus asked back, "Which of these three proved to be a neighbor?" In one sentence Jesus changed the question from What kind of person is my neighbor? to What kind of person am I becoming? Walk down the road below and watch the question turn around.
Love does not start by sorting people into those who qualify and those who do not. It sees, it feels, and it crosses the road.
1.3 - Who have you quietly kept on the other side of the road: someone different from you, hard to love, or easy to overlook?
The One Who Crossed Over to You

Jesus told this story to teach a proud man how to love. But it also points past itself to Jesus. Before you can love your neighbor like the Samaritan loved the wounded man, you have to see that the Samaritan in the story is Jesus, and the man on the side of the road is you. While you were still bruised by shame, still bleeding from your own choices, still left for dead by sin, Jesus crossed over. He did not pass by. He did not have more important religious work to attend to. He came down the road, knelt in the dust beside you, and bound up the wounds you could not bind up yourself.
The Samaritan paid for the man's care out of his own pocket. Jesus paid for yours with His own life. He did not just give what was required. He gave Himself.
but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

Mercy is not a virtue you take up on your strongest days. It is the air you have been breathing ever since Jesus came down to find you. When you move toward the bruised, the lonely, the unlikable, or the enemy, you are walking the same road He walked toward you. May the followers of Jesus look like the One they follow. Go and do likewise.
1.4 - Who has God placed in your path, on your street, at work, or at your regular stops, that you have been treating more like an interruption than an assignment? Write down one or two names.
This Week's Practice

Pick one of the names you just wrote down and do one costly thing for that person this week. Costly does not have to mean expensive. It means it costs you something in attention, time, or comfort. Learn their name. Ask a real question and stay long enough to hear the real answer. Bring them something they did not ask for. Then notice what God does in you when you move toward someone instead of past them.

Then read Luke 10:25-37 slowly, twice. Once as the priest who passes by, asking the Lord for courage to stop. Once as the wounded man on the road, letting it sink in that Jesus has already stopped for you.
Lesson 1 Review

Loving your neighbor is not a separate assignment from loving God. It is the same love pointed in a second direction. Jesus made your own self-love the measuring stick, summed it up in the Golden Rule, and through Paul called you to count others more significant than yourself. Then, through the Good Samaritan, He turned the question around, from Who qualifies for my love? to Who will I move toward? Because Jesus crossed the road to you, you can cross the road to others.
In the next lesson, you will bring this love home, to the first neighbors under your own roof.
Closing Reflections
What is one key thing you learned from this lesson?
What is one step you are going to take this week?
